title: Cyrus the Anointed and Salvation for the Ends of the Earth
summary: God addresses Cyrus as his anointed, promising to open gates before him and give him hidden treasures so that he, and all the world, may know that the LORD alone is God. God rebukes those who question his ways as clay questioning the potter, and declares that Cyrus will rebuild his city and free his exiles. The chapter widens to the nations, who will confess that God is with Israel, and ends with a universal invitation: every people is called to turn to God and be saved, and every knee will bow to him.
story: Chapter 44 ended by naming Cyrus. Chapter 45 speaks to him directly, and it is one of the most daring passages in the Old Testament: a Persian king who does not know the LORD is called his anointed and his chosen instrument. The prophet anticipates that some in Israel will object (verses 9 to 13), and he answers them. Then the chapter moves beyond Israel's release to the whole world. The logic of Isaiah 40 to 48, that the LORD alone is God, reaches its widest conclusion here: if there is only one God, then salvation must be offered to every nation.
historical:
Cyrus's conquest of Babylon in 539 BC was remarkably swift. Babylonian records, including the document known as the Nabonidus Chronicle, report that his forces entered the city without a battle, after the last Babylonian king, Nabonidus, had lost the support of many in the city. The Greek historian Herodotus later described the massive walls of Babylon with gates of bronze, which gives vivid background to verse 2, whatever the exact details. The “treasures of darkness” in verse 3 recalls the famous wealth of the kingdoms Cyrus conquered, especially Lydia, whose king Croesus was proverbial for his riches, and Babylon itself.

Cyrus's own inscriptions credit his success to Marduk, the chief god of Babylon, which confirms what verses 4 and 5 say twice: “though you have not known Me.” The chapter does not claim that Cyrus converted. It claims that the God of Israel was working through him whether he knew it or not.
cultural:
Anointing with oil was the ceremony by which Israel's priests and especially its kings were set apart for office. “The LORD's anointed” was a title of the kings of David's line, which makes its use for a Persian king startling. The Hebrew word is mashiach, from which the English “Messiah” comes, though in the Old Testament it usually means simply a person consecrated for a task. Grasping someone's right hand was a gesture of support and installation; in Babylon, a king was said to take the hand of the god in the New Year festival.

The potter and the clay (verse 9) was an image every ancient reader knew. Potters worked in every town, shaping clay on a wheel, and a pot that argued with its maker was absurd. The image of verse 14, peoples of Egypt, Cush, and Seba coming in chains and bowing, uses the language of ancient tribute processions, but the point of their confession is that the God of Israel is the only God. Swearing by one's own self (verse 23) was the strongest oath possible, since there was no one greater to swear by.
literary: The chapter has three movements. Verses 1 to 8 are a royal oracle to Cyrus, the kind of speech a god might address to a king at his installation, framed by the repeated claim “I am the LORD, and there is no other” and closing with a short hymn calling heaven and earth to produce righteousness and salvation. Verses 9 to 13 are a disputation against objectors, built on two woes and a pointed question. Verses 14 to 25 turn to the nations and move toward the climactic invitation of verse 22. The phrase “there is no other” or its equivalent appears again and again through the chapter, like a drumbeat.

outline.t: God's word to Cyrus, his anointed
Woe to the clay that argues with the potter
The nations confess that God is with Israel
The God who speaks openly and alone foretells
Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth

doctrines.note: God raises Cyrus, opens gates before him, and equips him for battle, all for the sake of Israel and so that the world may know the LORD. The chapter holds that God directs even rulers who do not acknowledge him.

“I am the LORD, and there is no other.” The chapter repeats this claim more than any other in the Bible. Its consequence is that the God of Israel is not a local deity but the Creator of all, and so the only Savior.

“Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.” If there is only one God, then his salvation is offered to every people. Verse 22 is one of the clearest universal invitations in the Old Testament.

Salvation is described as righteousness sprouting from the earth, as an everlasting deliverance, and as justification: “In the LORD all descendants of Israel will be justified.” It comes from God and is received by turning to him.

words.note: Mashiach, anointed one, the source of the word Messiah. In the Old Testament it is used for kings, priests, and once here for a foreign ruler. It marks a person as set apart by God for a task. Only later did the word become a title for the expected king of David's line, which is why the New Testament calls Jesus the Christ, the Greek form of the same idea.

Ra, bad or evil, here translated “calamity.” It is the opposite of shalom (well-being) in the same verse. The word covers moral evil but also disaster and harm, and in context it refers to the calamities that fall on nations, such as the fall of Babylon.

Satar, to hide. “Truly You are a God who hides Himself.” The verse acknowledges that God's ways are not obvious: he works through a pagan king and through exile. Later Christian theology made much of the idea of the hidden God, the God who acts in unexpected ways.
Panah, to turn. “Turn to Me and be saved.” The word describes a change of direction and attention. Salvation is offered as something the nations can receive by turning to the one God.

christ: The New Testament draws directly on this chapter. Paul quotes verse 23 in Romans 14:11 to say that every knee will bow before God, and in Philippians 2:10-11 he applies the same words to Jesus: at the name of Jesus every knee will bow and every tongue confess that he is Lord. In Isaiah, that homage belongs to the LORD alone, so Paul's use is a strong statement of Christ's full deity. Paul also takes up the image of the potter and the clay in Romans 9:20-21. The title anointed, used here of Cyrus, finds its full meaning in Jesus, the Christ (the Anointed One), who brings a greater release than Cyrus did. Finally, the universal invitation of verse 22 anticipates the gospel's going out to the ends of the earth, which the New Testament presents as the fulfillment of God's intention to save people of every nation.

hard.q: Does verse 7 mean that God creates evil?
hard.a:
Older English translations, such as the King James Version, have God say in verse 7 that he creates evil, which has troubled many readers. Most interpreters agree that the Hebrew word ra here means calamity or disaster, the opposite of shalom (well-being) in the same line, not moral wickedness. In context, God is claiming that the rise and fall of nations, including the disaster that will fall on Babylon and the prosperity that will come to Israel, are in his hands. Some interpreters suggest the verse also answers a dualistic view of the world, like the one later associated with Persian religion, in which good and evil are rival powers. Isaiah allows no second power.

This does not settle every question about God and evil. Scripture elsewhere insists that God is not the author of sin (James 1:13) while also holding that nothing happens outside his rule. Christians have held these together in different ways, with some stressing God's active ordaining of all things and others stressing his permission of what he does not cause. The verse itself is about God's sovereignty over history, and it is meant as comfort: no dark power can overturn God's purpose.

questions: God used Cyrus, who did not know him. Where have you seen God work through people or events that seemed to have nothing to do with him?
Verse 15 says God hides himself. How do you hold together God's hiddenness and his invitation to “Turn to Me and be saved”?
Paul applied Isaiah's “every knee will bow” to Jesus. What does that tell you about who the early Christians believed Jesus to be?
